title: TTPO: Training at Test Time Without Labels
hook: Majority voting is a fragile teacher — one bad vote poisons every token. TTPO exploits an asymmetry: rollouts that disagree with the vote are usually wrong even when the vote is too.
key_points: RL and on-policy self-distillation need ground-truth labels, which rules out test-time training.
Majority-vote pseudo-labels are the obvious substitute but are fragile: a wrong vote corrupts the teacher signal.
Key observation: the failure is asymmetric — disagreeing rollouts are typically wrong regardless of whether the vote is right.
TTPO distils agreeing rollouts via OPSD and penalizes disagreeing rollouts with grouped RL.
Token-level selection refines both: distillation down-weights converged positions, RL penalizes only confident errors.
Label-free, it matches label-supervised OPSD on five competition benchmarks and lifts Qwen3-1.7B from 38.0% to 45.2%.
content_html: Post-training methods that work — RL with verifiable rewards, on-policy self-distillation — all need labels. That blocks test-time training, where you would like a model to improve on the very problems it is currently facing. The natural workaround is majority voting over rollouts, and it is brittle: if the vote is wrong, the teacher is wrong, and every token gets pulled the wrong way.
extra_html:
The insight

Wang and colleagues observe that the failure mode is asymmetric. Rollouts that disagree with the majority label are usually wrong — not just when the vote is right, but also when it is wrong. Agreement is weak evidence of correctness; disagreement is much stronger evidence of error. So the two groups deserve different objectives.

TTPO distils the agreeing rollouts with on-policy self-distillation, and penalizes the disagreeing ones with grouped RL. Token-level selection then refines each branch: distillation down-weights positions that have already converged, and the RL penalty applies only to confident errors. Both updates stay well-grounded even when pseudo-labels are frequently wrong, and majority-vote routing tightens as the model improves.

Results

Without any labels, TTPO matches label-supervised OPSD on five competition-level benchmarks, raises Qwen3-1.7B from 38.0% to 45.2% in test-time training, reports +25.2 to +36.4 points in the no-thinking setting, and generalizes across tasks. The transferable idea is the design pattern: when a noisy signal is asymmetrically noisy, split it and use each half where it is reliable.

related.title: One Symptom, Three Levers: A Critical Review of On-Policy Self-Distillation
related.hook: Self-distillation drops the costly teacher by letting a model teach itself with privileged information. The asymmetry that creates the signal also biases it — into collapse.

related.title: Evolution Strategies Beat GRPO on Reasoning Coverage
related.hook: GRPO sharpens one answer and collapses entropy. Evolution strategies keep the population diverse — improving pass@1 while also raising pass@k, which GRPO gives up.

flashcards.prompt: What asymmetry lets TTPO survive wrong majority votes?
flashcards.back_html: Rollouts that disagree with the pseudo-label are typically wrong whether or not the vote itself is correct. So penalizing disagreement is safe even when trusting the vote as a teacher would not be.

flashcards.prompt: How does TTPO treat the two groups of rollouts differently?

choices.text: Agreeing rollouts are distilled; disagreeing rollouts are penalized with grouped RL
Both groups are distilled, weighted by vote share
Disagreeing rollouts are discarded and only agreeing ones are used

flashcards.explanation_html: The two branches use different objectives precisely because the reliability of the signal differs: agreement is weak evidence of correctness, disagreement is strong evidence of error.

flashcards.prompt: What does TTPO achieve without any ground-truth labels?
flashcards.back_html: It matches label-supervised OPSD across five competition-level benchmarks, and raises Qwen3-1.7B from 38.0% to 45.2% in the test-time-training setting.
